title: More Area, Less Coffee Per Hectare? Reconciling Expansion and Productivity in Nepal Coffee Sector, 1994–2025
content: Nepal’s coffee sector is promoted as a high-value, climate sensitive opportunity for mid-hill smallholders, yet its progress is usually judged by planted area. We harmonise official statistics spanning three decades a national series (1994/95–2013/14), five later national observations (2014/15–2024/25) and district tables for 2013/14 and 2024/25 and triangulate them against FAO yields, trade records and a recent plot level study. Reported plantation area grew from 136 ha to 5,501 ha (10.1% yr⁻¹ after 2013/14), whereas green bean output reached only 642 t; yield on plantation area fell from about 225 kg ha⁻¹ (2013/14) to 117 kg ha⁻¹ (2024/25), 17.5% of Ethiopia’s FAO reported yield. Between 2000/01 and 2013/14, production moved one-for-one with area (elasticity 1.01, R² = 0.94) and yield showed no trend (p = 0.74), a pattern consistent with area-derived production estimates. In 24 matched districts, median yield fell from 238 to 111 kg ha⁻¹ (21 declines; Wilcoxon p < 0.001), but the fall was unrelated to expansion speed (Spearman ρ = -0.05) and occurred in all six slowly expanding districts, which weakens an immature plantation explanation. Three districts (Kavre, Nuwakot, Ilam) supply 46% of output, and Koshi Province holds 31.5% of area but 20.0% of output. Meeting claimed demand of 6,000–8,000 t would need 51,000–69,000 ha at today’s reported yield but 12,000–22,000 ha at plot-level yields of 364–486 kg ha⁻¹. Nepal’s coffee constraint is therefore productivity and measurement rather than land. We propose a bearing area census and plot-level monitoring as preconditions for evidence-based coffee policy.
